An explosive report has revealed that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries held a secret meeting with Trump administration power broker Jared Kushner to find “common ground” with the far right in the past weeks — as he made statements that could isolate the left-wing members of the House Democratic Caucus.
The New York Times reported on Sunday that the two recently met in a space offered by a mutual friend in New York City, citing two people familiar with the meeting and another who was briefed on it. The meeting covered a broad range of topics for the two men who have been in contact since collaborating on a criminal legal system reform bill in Donald Trump’s first term.
The meeting appears to be an acknowledgement that Democrats are expected to win control of the House this November, and that Jeffries is likely to become speaker.
One theme of their conversation was to find “common ground” on issues like housing, the high cost of living, and immigration. On those topics, Kushner suggested that Jeffries meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.
The report did not specify whether the two came to any agreements on those topics. However, it comes as the Trump administration’s war with Israel on Iran is drastically raising prices across all sectors — a war that Jeffries has opposed, but in a relatively muted way.
It also comes as the Trump administration has pursued extreme policies on immigration. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have arrested and detained a record number of people in Trump’s second term, conducting raids targeted at Democratic-leaning areas, while officials are also meting out harsh punishments for anyone opposed to the mass deportation campaign.
Many Democratic voters oppose ICE and Trump’s raids. But, as outrage spread over the administration’s ICE crackdowns earlier this year, Jeffries only said he would advocate for minor reforms to the agency’s conduct — and refused to whip against the DHS funding bill earlier this year.
Republicans downplayed the meeting after it sparked furor on the right, with House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) saying that Kushner is “not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House” — though he has served as a representative of the Trump administration in critical affairs like in negotiations with Israel over colonialist plans for Gaza and the war on Iran.
Facing fierce criticism from the report of the meeting, meanwhile, Jeffries said in a statement that the Republicans’ “extremist approach” to governance in this Congress “will be met with forceful opposition.”
“In every conversation that we have with the Trump administration, we will continue to make it explicitly clear that the affordability crisis is not a hoax and nothing short of transformational policy change is acceptable,” Jeffries said.
However, it is “transformational policy change” that Jeffries has worked to oppose and obstruct from left-wing members of his caucus.
For instance, last week, Jeffries said that, despite his support in previous years, he now opposes Medicare for All during an interview on NBC. He said, instead, that Democrats are working to “make health care affordable” for all, without specifying how. Other priorities that may be championed by progressives — like impeachment of Trump or his cabinet, abolishing ICE, or cutting aid to Israel — have also gotten the cold shoulder from Jeffries in recent weeks.
In the NBC interview, Jeffries would not say whether or not he believes that democratic socialists have a place in the Democratic Party — despite multiple Democratic Socialists of America members holding seats in his caucus and others running for highly contested seats in Congress. In June, Jeffries put distance between himself and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, saying that Mamdani has “work to do” to placate more centrist members of Congress.
Jeffries’s comments reignited calls for him to step down as House Democratic leader. However, unlike Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Jeffries has not faced a major push to be unseated.

Jeffries, Kushner meet as Trump eyes loss of House
The meeting of House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner points to the White House’s concerns about losing majority control in the midterms
What happened
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) and Jared Kushner, a top outside adviser to his father-in-law, President Donald Trump, “met privately in recent weeks” and “discussed potential areas of common ground,” The New York Times reported Sunday.
The meeting “shows the depth of Republican Party angst over losing their congressional majority,” The Associated Press said, and White House efforts to “stem any potential political fallout” on Trump if Democrats “wrest majority control” in November.
Who said what
Kushner and Jeffries “discussed housing, immigration and the high cost of living,” the Times said, all issues where compromise “seems remote.” The Trump GOP’s “my-way-or-the-highway approach to governing” has “failed the American people,” Jeffries said Sunday, and the “question is whether Republicans will join us” in “fighting for an affordable America.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) “bristled” Sunday when asked about the meeting, the AP said. “I don’t know what that’s about,” but Kushner “hedges his bets” and isn’t “directly involved” in “day-to-day” White House operations, he said on Fox News. “I’m telling you, we’re going to defy history and hold this majority.”

Trump Camp Braces for GOP House Defeat After Jared Kushner's Secret Meeting With Hakeem Jeffries
Jared Kushner's quiet outreach to Hakeem Jeffries has Washington buzzing, as a Democratic House takeover could leave Trump facing subpoenas, investigations and even impeachment pressure
A private meeting between Jared Kushner and Hakeem Jeffries in New York has sparked fresh questions about whether President Donald Trump's inner circle is preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of the House in the 2026 midterm elections.
The Jared Kushner-Hakeem Jeffries secret meeting, first reported by The New York Times, reportedly focused on housing, immigration, and the soaring cost of living, issues Democrats have made central to their campaign.
More significantly, Kushner suggested that Jeffries meet with White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles for a follow-up conversation, according to the report.
Why the Meeting Matters
The timing is hard to ignore. Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, could become speaker if Democrats regain control of the chamber in November. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority, meaning a relatively small number of competitive districts could determine who controls the House.
A Democratic House would dramatically change Trump's political landscape. Instead of relying on Republican lawmakers to advance his agenda, Trump could face an opposition-controlled chamber with the power to launch investigations, issue subpoenas, and conduct aggressive oversight of his administration.
Impeachment Could Become a Threat
That is where the story takes a much more explosive turn. If Democrats win the House, impeachment could become one of the constitutional tools available to them. Jeffries has repeatedly criticised Trump's administration and has spoken about holding the White House accountable, although Democrats have not made impeachment the centrepiece of their 2026 campaign.
Winning the House would not automatically trigger impeachment. But it would give Democrats significantly more power to investigate the president and his administration, potentially creating a political environment far more hostile to Trump. That makes the Hakeem Jeffries meeting Jared Kushner especially intriguing.
Johnson Fires Back
House Speaker Mike Johnson was quick to distance himself from the significance of the meeting.
Appearing on Fox News, Johnson said he did not know what Kushner's conversation with Jeffries was about and stressed that Kushner does not have a formal role in the administration's day-to-day operations.
But Johnson also delivered the most memorable line of the controversy. He said Kushner 'hedges his bets' before warning Americans not to count out House Republicans.
The remark adds another layer to the story. While Kushner was reportedly opening a channel to the Democrat who could become speaker, Johnson was publicly insisting that Republicans still have a path to victory.
Kushner and Jeffries Have History
The two New Yorkers are not strangers. During Trump's first administration, Kushner and Jeffries worked together on criminal justice reform, including the First Step Act, which Trump signed into law in 2018. Their relationship survived years of political conflict between Trump and Democratic leaders.
That history means the Jared Kushner secret meeting does not necessarily prove that Trump's team expects Republicans to lose. It could instead reflect a pragmatic effort to maintain relationships across the political divide. Still, the timing makes the conversation difficult to dismiss.
Trump's Unusual Political Position
Kushner's role makes the meeting even more unusual. Although he has no formal White House position, Trump's son-in-law remains an influential outside adviser and has been involved in diplomatic efforts during Trump's second term.
Now he appears to be helping maintain a line of communication with Jeffries, while potentially connecting him with Wiles. That stands in sharp contrast to Trump's own relationship with the Democratic leader.
Trump has repeatedly attacked Jeffries politically, making Kushner's willingness to engage with him a notable departure from the president's combative approach.
Democrats See an Opening
Republicans are betting heavily on Trump's popularity with their core supporters to protect the Republican House majority.
Johnson has argued that the GOP can defy the historical pattern of the president's party losing ground during midterms. Democrats see the situation differently.
They are campaigning heavily on inflation, affordability, and dissatisfaction with the direction of the country, while targeting vulnerable Republican-held districts. The Senate is also becoming increasingly competitive.
A Democratic House takeover would therefore represent far more than a change in leadership. It could fundamentally alter the balance of power between Congress and the White House.
A Warning Sign for Trump?
There is no evidence that Trump or his inner circle has accepted a Republican defeat. But the meeting sends a revealing signal. Kushner is talking privately with the Democrat who could become speaker, and he reportedly wants Jeffries to sit down with the White House chief of staff. At the same time, Johnson is publicly warning Republicans not to bet against themselves.
If Democrats win in November, those conversations could suddenly look like early preparation for a radically different Washington. For now, the GOP still controls the House. But the 2026 midterm elections are turning into a test of whether Trump can keep Congress behind him, or whether Jeffries will soon have the power to hold his administration to account.

How Jared Kushner Snookered Hakeem Jeffries
Democrats need a fighter, but the congressional leader is addicted to illusory comity.
On Sunday, The New York Times reported that “Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, met privately in recent weeks with Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and top outside adviser, and discussed potential areas of common ground.” On one level, the meeting was clearly good news for Jeffries. The midterm elections will be held just 71 days from now, and there is every possibility that the Democrats could take control of the House and make Jeffries the next House Speaker. The fact that Kushner, who holds no official position but functions as the president’s consigliere, met with Jeffries is a sign that the White House is seriously contemplating such a defeat.
Not surprisingly, congressional Republicans are unhappy. Current House Speaker Mike Johnson tried to pooh-pooh the meeting and minimize Kushner’s importance, telling Fox News, “I don’t know what that’s about. I know Jared has interest in lots of other things going on.” Johnson added that Kushner “hedges bets” and is “not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House.”
It’s hard not to be delighted by Johnson’s discomfort. But the meeting also raised red flags for those who worried that Jeffries was helping whitewash one of Trump’s most corrupt cronies. Tommy Vietor, the former Obama adviser who cohosts the Pod Save America podcast, noted, “Jared Kushner has no actual government job he just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals. The only way [Jeffries] should work with him is with demands for documents and subpoenas.” Mehdi Hasan, the CEO of Zeteo, echoed Vietor, writing, “The only meeting Hakeem Jeffries should be having with Jared Kushner is to tell him he’ll be subpoenaed by the House for a corruption investigation on day one of Democratic control of the House. This is just pathetic stuff from the House Dem leader.” Erstwhile neocon turned anti-Trumper William Kristol posted, “Really? Or, as the kids say, AYFKM?” (The acronym stands for “Are you fucking kidding me?”)
Between them, the progressive Hasan, the Obama liberal Vietor, and the former neoconservative Kristol represent very different wings of the Democratic coalition. But they were all united in their alarm over the Kushner-Jeffries sit-down.
Still, the House Democratic leader found his defenders among the centrist establishment, with Neera Tanden, CEO of the Center for American Progress, predictably emerging as the congressional leader’s most forceful defender on social media.
Responding to a Jeffries critic, Tanden wrote, “Ask Mike Johnson how he feels about Trump White House admitting Dems are going to win the House before everyone loses it on this website.” Tanden also compared the Jeffries-Kushner private meeting with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s public meeting with Donald Trump last year.
But this is a spurious parallel. As journalist Brian Beutler, who writes at the Off Message Substack, notes,
Mamdani’s goal is to reduce harm to NYC. Jeffries is about to lead a coequal branch of the federal government under hostile occupation. I had mixed feelings about the Mamdani meeting (much as I enjoyed the pictures). This is worse…. Mamdani has almost no power over Trump; Jeffries will have a great deal over Trump, but not if he’s working cooperatively with him (as opposed to adversarially) on the issues he and Kushner reportedly discussed.
Strangely, Tanden undercut her own support for Jeffries by re-tweeting a poor defense from an anonymous account on X.com called “Scary Lawyerguy” noting that the Times report was cowritten by Maggie Haberman, famed for her extensive access to Trumpworld. This post speculated, “Trump’s son-in-law leaked to Maggie that he met privately with Jeffries as a means of stoking intra-party discord among Democrats.” Although meant to exonerate Jeffries, this theory makes him look bad, as someone who was successfully played by Kushner.
Leaving aside the murky matter of whether Kushner leaked the news of the meeting, the president’s son-in-law clearly outfoxed Jeffries. If he becomes speaker of the House, Jeffries will have to tackle the issue of Trump’s corruption. As my Nation colleague Chris Lehmann has cogently argued, House Democrats have been maddeningly reluctant to make the president’s crookedness a top political priority, preferring vague rhetoric about “kitchen sink” issues.
This myopia on corruption is especially frustrating because it has fueled Trump’s sense of invulnerability. The penny-ante pelf of his first term has been replaced by world-historical grifting, with the president and his family enriching themselves with billions of dollars in business deals.
No one in Trump’s inner circle embodies this naked venality more than Jared Kushner, who acts as an ambassador without portfolio, negotiating with countries in the Middle East, while also being enriched by deals with autocrats in the region.
In 2021, Kushner founded the investment firm Affinity Partners, which has received $2 billion in funding from the Saudi state as well as another $1.5 from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. Writing in The Atlantic, Andrea Bernstein noted that Kushner has been given a unique post that evades transparency:
While carrying out public business for his father-in-law, he has continued to pursue his private interests and declined to disclose any information about them. There’s a carve-out designation in ethics laws known as the “special government employee,” which allows businesspeople to perform work for the government. Elon Musk was a special government employee, and so was Corey Lewandowski. But Kushner has not been designated one. He is both outside and inside government—a “volunteer,” the White House calls him. And he is vaulting over strictures that were put in place to defend the mechanisms of government from becoming tools of foreign or private interests….
[Kushner] has a direct line to the president. But his political dealings are ineluctably intertwined with his businesses. Kushner is related by marriage to the president, one who smiles on those who do business with his family, and the 2021 Saudi investment in Affinity Partners was made despite the Saudi fund’s own finding that the company’s operations were “unsatisfactory in all aspects.” Kushner has defended the deal, saying that the Saudi fund “is one of the most prestigious investors in the world.”

If the Democrats win the House, Kushner’s many conflicts of interest should be a major focus of investigation. Unfortunately, Jeffries’s meeting with Kushner indicates that this is unlikely to happen, since Jeffries seems to think the president’s son-in-law is someone worth negotiating with.
Worryingly, Jeffries seems to have been motivated by positive memories of working with Kushner during Trump’s first term. As the Times reports, “The private get-together was described by one of the people as a catch-up for Mr. Kushner and Mr. Jeffries. The two men have stayed in touch since they worked together on a criminal justice bill midway through Mr. Trump’s first term.”
There’s an argument to be made—although one that requires an extraordinary generosity of spirit—that Kushner was a moderating influence on Trump’s first term. In truth, this claim rests more on PR spin than actual policy outcomes. But in Trump’s current term, Kushner is something different: an avatar of the president’s epic lawlessness. The fact that Jeffries can’t see that is disqualifying.
The Democrats need a fighter as their House leader. Instead, they have a collaborator, one who is loyal to dreams of comity even at the expense of tolerating corruption.

sources.news_title: Backlash After Hakeem Jeffries Holds Private Meeting With Jared Kushner Ahead of Midterms
sources.text:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries met privately with President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and adviser Jared Kushner in recent weeks, prompting criticism from some Democrats ahead of approaching midterm elections, according to reports.
Although Kushner, who served as a senior West Wing adviser during Trump’s first term, does not have a formal role in the current Administration, he has remained involved in Trump’s diplomatic efforts in the Middle East and Russia.
During the meeting, the pair were said to have discussed housing, immigration, and the high cost of living as potential areas of common ground.
The report comes less than three months before the November midterms, when Democrats are favored to retake control of the House from Republicans, who currently hold both chambers of Congress. A Democratic victory would put Jeffries in line to become speaker and give the party greater oversight powers to investigate the Trump Administration.
The meeting—an unusual instance of a top Democrat and a Trump confidant coming together to discuss potential areas of agreement—has drawn scrutiny from some within Democratic circles. It was first reported Sunday by The New York Times and has since been confirmed by multiple outlets.
“Throughout this Congress, Republicans have adopted a my-way-or-the-highway approach to governing that has failed the American people," Jeffries says in a statement to TIME. "To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition. The American people want bold change and that’s what House Democrats will deliver.”
“In every conversation that we have with the Trump administration, we will continue to make it explicitly clear that the affordability crisis is not a hoax and nothing short of transformational policy change is acceptable. We are fighting for an affordable America. The question is whether Republicans will join us,” the statement reads.
TIME has also reached out to the White House and Kushner for comment.
Asked whether he supported the meeting during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said: “I’m in favor of people meeting with whoever they want to discuss ideas. But it’s one thing to have a meeting. It’s another thing to see something real come out of that.”
Tommy Vietor, a former aide to President Barack Obama and now a co-host of the podcast Pod Save America, was far less diplomatic.
“Jared Kushner has no actual government job, he just uses his family connections to get money from Gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals. The only way Jeffries should work with him is with demands for documents and subpoenas,” Vietor said.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said Sunday that he first learned of the meeting that same day, when reports began circulating in the media.
"I don't know what that's about," Johnson said on Fox News. "I know Jared has interests and lots of other things going on. He's not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House."
Johnson, however, remained confident that Republicans could retain control of the House.
“I’m telling you what, you better not bet against the House Republicans,” he said.
Trump has met with the top Democratic leaders of the House and Senate only once since returning to office, when the President attempted last year to reach an agreement to prevent a government shutdown. Those talks ultimately failed, leading to the longest government shutdown in U.S. history.
The relationship between Trump, Jeffries, and other members of the Democratic leadership has often been marked by conflict and back-and-forth name-calling.
In late April, Trump called Jeffries a “low IQ person” and attacked Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer over their opposition to the Iran war, branding them “traitor Democrats.”
Jeffries, in turn, called Trump the “dumbest President ever” in response to the President’s insults during a press conference.
Trump has continued to attack the top House Democrat as "low IQ" and a "thug” branding him as a “danger” to the country.
More recently, however, Trump’s tone toward Jeffries appears to have softened. In an interview earlier this month with Punchbowl News, the President said he could work with the Democratic leader and described him as a "nice guy."
"People are harsh on me. I'm harsh on them. It's part of the world," Trump said. "I'd probably get along with him very well."
Since returning to the White House, Trump has often sought to bypass Congress and pursue policy through executive action, from curbing birthright citizenship to the implementation of tariffs.
That dynamic could change if Democrats take control of the House, where Republicans currently hold a slim majority of 218 Republicans to 212 Democrats and one independent.
A Democratic-controlled House would give the party the power to block parts of Trump’s legislative agenda, launch high-profile congressional investigations, issue subpoenas, and initiate impeachment proceedings.
Trump—who was impeached twice during his first term—has urged voters to back Republicans in the midterms, arguing that Democrats would use their power to impeach him again.
“I’m going to be impeached. They're going to impeach me. They have no idea why,” he told a crowd during a rally in South Carolina last Friday.
The latest Emerson College polling, released August 20, found congressional Democrats leading Republicans by nearly 8 points. A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll released Aug. 17 found Democrats ahead by 5 points. All 435 House seats are up for election in November.

sources.news_title: The structure of political revolutions
sources.text:
The structure of political revolutions
This is a followup to yesterday’s post about Hakeem Jefferies meeting with Jared Kushner covertly. The reactions to this development seemed to fall into two broad categories, which in turn reflected two fundamentally different perspectives on the current political situation.
Paradigm One: The Trump administration represents no significant threat to the maintenance of the political order, i.e., a liberal democracy operating under more or less recognizable legal and bureaucratic norms.
Paradigm Two: The Trump administration represents a significant threat to these things.
I’ll call this the difference between normal politics and revolutionary politics. At the beginning of the first Trump administration, almost all elite actors in the political, intellectual, and media spheres accepted Paradigm One as a matter of course, and treated the invocation of Paradigm Two as a species of hyperbole and hysteria.
Nearly halfway through the second Trump administration, the proportions have shifted quite markedly, but I’m still surprised how many people, including here at LGM, are still operating pretty much squarely within Paradigm One. Such people assume that, for example, Trump is going to honor the results of the 2026 and 2028 elections if he and his party lose, and that we will simply move on at that point from Trump and Trumpism, although of course he will spawn many imitators who try to replicate his success. Another way of thinking about this frame of mind is as the Biden model, because this was very much the implicit assumption of the Biden administration.
Again, I remain somewhat surprised this this model survived the events up to and culminating in January 6, 2021, but only somewhat, because of the overwhelming inertial power of standard political and cultural frames, and the understandable resistance to the idea that something genuinely disruptive and even revolutionary may be happening.
I’m trying to be fair and balanced here, and I recognize that this model might not actually be wrong, or not wholly so. It remains possible that Trump and the GOP will lose a wave election 75 days from now, and he and his minions won’t have the necessary coherence and organizational discipline to seriously contest that, and he will decide to give up on his current plans to stay in office after 1/20/2029, and King Leer will crawl unburdened towards death. I admit this is possible: I think it’s unlikely.
In short, I think we’re in a disjunctive, paradigm-shifting political and cultural situation, and that Trump does not intend to leave office, or to recognize the results of elections he loses, and that instead he and his inner circle intend to overthrow the current political system with some sort of authoritarian “managed democracy,” that retains the trappings of the old system superficially, but replaces it with a functional one-party state. I don’t know, of course, whether they can manage to succeed in this ambition, but I do believe it is their actual plan, on the basis of their words and deeds, both since 1/20/2025, and most particularly since 1/6/2021 — a day the events of an enormous number of elite actors continue to pretend did not actually happen, or at least did not happen in the way they did (see the Biden model of interpretation for these events).
These conflicting models of interpretation help explain why, for example, when LGMers say things like it’s good for Jeffries to meet with Kushner, because after all the Trump administration is going to have to work with the Democrats if and when the Democrats win the midterms, this kind of putative realpolitik strikes a lot of other people as fundamentally mistaken. This perspective assumes, at its core, that we are still operating within normal political parameters, subject no doubt to various idiosyncrasies of Trump and the Trumpist moment. But the assumption is that these idiosyncrasies are just that, and not signs and symptoms of some deeper disjunction.
The acid test for these conflicting interpretations is, I think, the question of whether Trump will attempt to remain in office. Paradigm One more or less assumes that either he won’t try, or if he does try it won’t go anywhere, because of The Rules. Paradigm Two assumes that he will try, and he might well be successful, because we have spent the last eleven years moving in fits and starts from normal politics into a revolutionary paradigm.
Again I want to emphasize that it’s not completely clear which of these paradigms is more accurate. I just want to point out that they’re both very much part of the conversation now, in a way in which one of them pretty much really wasn’t prior to 1/6/2021, and that when people talk past each other here and elsewhere it’s due in part to their usually implicit acceptance of one rather than the other of these different frames of understanding.

A private meeting between House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and influential outside adviser, is suddenly attracting attention in Washington with control of Congress hanging in the balance.
The two men met privately in New York in recent weeks and discussed several of the most politically explosive issues facing the country, including housing, immigration and the cost of living, according to reports Sunday.
But the most consequential detail may be what reportedly came next.
Kushner suggested that Jeffries meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles as a follow-up, according to The Associated Press. That raises the possibility that the Trump orbit is already establishing lines of communication with the Democrat who could become the next speaker of the House if his party wins control of the chamber in November.
The timing is impossible to ignore. The midterm elections are less than three months away. Republicans are fighting to protect a narrow House majority, Democrats believe the chamber is within reach, and a change in control would fundamentally reshape the final two years of Trump’s second term.
Jeffries and Kushner Quietly Find Common Ground

Kushner himself could potentially become a subject of Democratic scrutiny.
The Guardian noted that House Judiciary Committee Democrats opened an investigation earlier this year concerning possible conflicts between Kushner’s overseas diplomatic work and his private business interests.
That makes the political dynamic even more unusual: Kushner is talking about cooperation with a party whose lawmakers could soon have vastly greater power to investigate Trump’s administration and inner circle.

Republican leaders cannot publicly behave as though defeat is inevitable while they are campaigning to retain control of Congress.
The White House, however, also has an interest in being prepared for every possible result.
Those two objectives are not necessarily contradictory.
A Meeting About More Than November
The safest interpretation of the Jeffries-Kushner meeting is not that a grand bipartisan alliance is suddenly forming.
There is no evidence of that.
Instead, the conversation may reveal something more practical about how Washington operates when political power is uncertain.
Trump’s second-term relationship with congressional Democrats has been extraordinarily combative. But if Democrats win the House, neither side will be able to completely ignore the other.
Government funding, economic legislation, national-security measures and other must-pass bills could require negotiations.
At the same time, a Democratic House would have the ability to investigate the administration in ways Republicans currently do not.
That gives both camps a reason to understand the other before Election Day.
For Jeffries, talking to Kushner offers a channel into Trump’s inner circle without making any public concessions to the president.
For Kushner and potentially the White House, talking to Jeffries creates a line to the man who could become one of the most powerful figures in Washington.
Neither side has to trust the other for that relationship to be useful.
The Midterms Have Already Changed Washington
November’s elections have not happened yet, but the possibility of a Democratic House is already affecting behavior in Washington.
Republicans are publicly projecting confidence. Democrats are preparing for the possibility of governing.
And somewhere between those competing realities, Jared Kushner and Hakeem Jeffries have quietly begun talking.
Whether the meeting ultimately produces cooperation, confrontation or nothing at all remains unknown.
But Kushner’s reported suggestion that Jeffries carry on the conversation with Trump’s chief of staff makes one thing clear: powerful figures on both sides are thinking seriously about what Washington could look like the morning after the midterms.
And they are apparently not waiting until November to prepare for it.

“To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition,” the New York congressman said. “The question is whether Republicans will join us.”
The meeting shows the depth of Republican Party angst over losing their congressional majority, particularly the House, and the need to make inroads with the opposing party as the White House seeks to stem any potential political fallout on the president.
If Democrats retake power, the White House can expect an aggressive oversight agenda into what Jeffries has called the “crooks” in the administration, with the threat of impeachment among the many tools at the party’s disposal.

Kushner is a familiar Trump emissary to Democrats
Jeffries and Kushner are not strangers.
The New Yorkers allied during the first Trump administration on landmark legislation to allow sentencing flexibility for certain drug offenses as a way to curtail lengthy terms in the federal prison system.
While not necessarily close, the two have maintained a relationship despite the repeated attacks Trump has leveled against Jeffries and the Democratic leader’s responses. In Trump’s second term, Kushner has an oversize role despite having no formal position in the White House. He serves as an outside adviser and envoy, particularly shuttling to foreign diplomatic missions as the U.S. war against Iran drags into its sixth month.
Trump has only met with Jeffries once since the president returned to the White House, taunting the House leader and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York with red “Make America Great Again” 2028 caps on the desk in front of them in the Oval Office — a nod to Trump’s toying with an unconstitutional third term in office.
After that fall meeting, Trump posted a fake image of Schumer with Jeffries wearing a sombrero with a handlebar mustache in what was widely viewed as a racist trope as he mocked the Democrats before what became the longest federal government shutdown in U.S. history.
Trump has been able to alternately ignore the Congress as he relies on the sheer force of executive power to implement his priorities or to pressure the Republicans in the House and Senate, when needed, to fall in line behind the White House, particularly to confirm controversial Cabinet nominees.
All that is likely to change if Democrats control either chamber, with lawmakers eager for Congress to flex their own power as a coequal branch of government more willing to hold the White House in check.
Republicans and Democrats race for power in midterms
House Republicans are counting on Trump’s popularity among their core voters as they struggle to hold onto majority control, with Johnson believing the GOP will defy history that tends to reward the challengers in midterms and punish the party in power.
The House GOP has a slim majority. Control will likely be won — or lost — in a handful of battleground districts as Democrats put forward candidates in what they hope will be something of a repeat of 2018, when they swept to power riding a wave of voter unrest during Trump’s first term.
While the House is most at risk for Republicans this year, he narrowly split Senate is also increasingly in play. GOP strategists worry about an enthusiasm gap on their side as Democrats appear more eager to head to the polls.
At the same time, Democrats are nominating outsider candidates, some aligned with socialist agendas over establishment backed candidates, in a sign of voter unrest with the status quo.
